title: Edible wafer-paper flowers for cake decoration
subtitle: How to cut and shape rice-paper petals into lightweight flowers
excerpt: Wafer paper flowers are cut from edible rice paper, shaped while slightly dampened, and left to dry in petal moulds or foil cups. They are much lighter than sugar paste flowers and suit informal, layered cake designs where gumpaste sculpture would look too formal. A basic set of flower cutters, a damp brush, and a wire drying rack are all that is needed.
sourceNotes: Wafer-paper flowers are a contemporary cake-decorating technique using edible rice paper (oblatne or wafer paper) as the medium.

recipe.yieldDescription: 10 to 12 medium flowers (for one layer cake)
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Finished flowers keep for 2 weeks in an airtight box away from moisture. Do not refrigerate.

glossaryTerms.definition: Thin edible sheets made from potato starch, water, and oil. Also called rice paper or oblatne. Sold in sheets and available in standard white or pre-coloured. Absorbs moisture quickly and shapes when lightly dampened.

content.text: cut into petal shapes, curled while damp, and dried in a cupped mould. They are much lighter than gumpaste flowers and create a softly layered, natural-looking bloom rather than a sculpted one.

Wafer paper sheets (A4, standard weight), petal cutters or sharp scissors, a damp pastry brush, small cups or crumpled foil for drying moulds, edible paint or food colouring thinned with vodka (optional, for colouring the petals). Handle wafer paper quickly; it becomes limp when exposed to air moisture for too long.

Cut petal shapes from the dry wafer paper using cutters or scissors. For a basic open flower, cut five to eight petals per flower, each 3 to 5 cm long. Wafer paper is fragile at the edges and tears if cut with a blunt tool; use a sharp craft knife on a silicone mat for precise shapes.

Brush the back of each petal very lightly with water. The paper becomes pliable in seconds. Curl the edges slightly upward between your fingers to create a natural curve. Overlap the base of the petals and press together while damp to assemble the flower. Place in a foil cup or crumpled tissue to hold the layered shape while it dries. Drying takes 1 to 2 hours at room temperature.

Paint the petals with edible colour after they are dry, using food colouring diluted in a small amount of clear spirit (vodka evaporates cleanly). A light wash builds up gradually; deep colour requires several layers. Brush from the tip toward the centre for a natural graduation.

Press the completed flowers gently into the frosted cake surface. They will stand on their own if the frosting is firm. For a floating arrangement, insert a small dab of buttercream under the base of each flower to secure it. Arrange in clusters for best effect.
